#2.6d Averaging smooths out the data and makes it harder to see trends. It does appear to be seasonal. You can see that the volume is higher in the summer quarters and lower in the winter quarters

#2.7b At the end of every year, there is a drop. It seems to be a steep rise in summer, then a drop through Fall and Winter. The SA series is smoother and has less variation than the NSA series. The trend stays practically the same throughout the entire series.

#2.7d I added geom_smooth to the plot to show the trend more clearly. The trend shows a general increase in gasoline sales over time

Transformations

#3.1a The swings grow from 1960 to 1985, then they start to decrease.

#3.1b The shape changed to a typical logarithmic curve. The seasonal swings are less pronounced in the log graph, but still noticeable. I don’t think the log transformation is a good idea. The only noticeable difference is the shape of the trend.

#3.1c The case for logging this series is stronger because it becomes more linear than when logging the other series.

#3.2 The log difference approximation is more appropriate for this series because it is less affected by the large swings in the data.

#3.3 The adjusted series is much smoother and has less extreme swings. The not adjusted data is noisier because it has more variation and has the seasonal drop every year.

#4.1b The seasonally adjusted series has a much smoother line and trend compared to the NSA series. You can see the variation by the amount of dips in the NSA data.

#4.1c I can see a seasonal decline starting in the Spring, continuing through the Summer, then a rise in the Fall, and then declining again in the winter. This makes sense because of things such as heating a house during the cold months

#4.3a The month with the largest seasonal factor seems to be December. It is roughly 0.2 over the trend and the size of the swings seem to decrease over time.

#4.3b The appear to be fairly similar. The big difference is 2020 to 2023.

#4.4a The estimated average monthly growth rate of gas production is 0.4% The month with the most significant seasonal effect is June

#4.4b #the tracks fit the actual series not well seeing as the actual #line is not linear

#4.4c The residuals do not look like white noise. The p value tells us that we reject the null hypothesis of no autocorrelation

#5.1a The dates of the first and last forecast are January 1980 and March 2005. snaive forecasts more accurately and the metrics agree based on the low values

#5.2a The DM statistic is -31.278 and the p-value is 2.2e-16. The p value tell us there is a statistical significance in the difference between the models

#5.3a snaive MAE is 0.562 and RMSE is 0.702. tslm MAE is 2.09 and RMSE is 2.42 the tslm model’s accuracy changed more when switching methods. This is due to the rolling window only using more recent data rather than using all data, which would skew results.

Reflection

The Ljung Box test had a p value of 0 meaning there was a lot of autocorrelation in the residuals and they did not behave like white noise. The forecast showed that the snaive model was better than the tslm model. The snaive model had lower MAE and RMSE values, this suggests that trend and model were missing important patterns in the data. I would expect a better model to have residuals with little to no effect on the line.
